I have been farming these lands for 40 years, and I know what works in Quzhou. My household has seven mouths, and with some of the younger ones working in the city, labor is tight, so I cannot take too many risks. I have 10.9 mu in total. I will put 8 mu into my wheat-maize rotation—that is my bread and butter. The wheat goes in after the autumn harvest, sleeps through the winter, and comes up strong in spring; then right after I cut the wheat in early June, I plant the maize. The other 2.9 mu I will plant to cotton. Cotton is more work, especially the spraying, but the price has been decent and my wife and I can manage that much.

For the wheat, I will use an improved variety I have planted for years—it gives around 1000 jin per mu if the water holds. I will rotary-till before sowing, put down about 35 kg of nitrogen per mu and a good dose of compound fertilizer for phosphorus and potassium, and irrigate four times from reviving to grain filling. I have my own well, so water is not a problem. I will spray three or four times for insects and weeds.

For the summer maize, I buy hybrid seed from the dealer—something like Nongda or Denghai. I plant it right after the wheat comes off, usually no-till or with light rotary work to save time and fuel. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat but still wants nitrogen. Two irrigations are usually enough if the summer rains cooperate, and I spray for pests a few times.

The cotton is sown in late April. I use an improved cotton seed, rotary-till the plot, and fertilize with a bit less nitrogen but more potassium to keep the bolls healthy. Cotton pests are relentless here, so I will spray more than a dozen times through the season. I irrigate three times when the dry spells hit.

I keep some of the wheat for our own flour and sell the rest, along with all the maize and cotton. That is how I have always balanced food security and cash income, and I see no reason to change it this year.
